title: The Second Paramita: Sila
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of cultivating a compassionate and generous heart through the practice of ethics, rather than simply avoiding wrongdoing. By studying the 16 Bodhisattva precepts, practitioners can develop a more nuanced understanding of ethics that prioritizes kindness, respect, and love towards all beings. This approach encourages flexibility and discernment in applying the precepts, letting go of grudges and old stories to live ethically with greater ease and freedom.

sentences.text: Thanks everyone, and thank you all for coming in out of the blue sky this morning.

I was thinking I drove up from Marble Mount early this morning, and between the pouring rain yesterday afternoon and the stars that just broke out at night, and then driving out of clouds into fog and then up to this blue sky—what a place we live, it's quite remarkable.

I always have a backup paper copy when I use my iPad because the day I got this green rakusu, I pulled my iPad out to give my talk and it was in the process of rebooting, not to be disturbed, so I had to make it all up, but you know that's kind of what we're doing.
So Buddhism loves lists, as do many other organizations.
In this case, the list I'm going to draw from is the six paramitas.
Paramita is about wisdom, so basically it's a grouping of the five qualities that combine together to make the sixth paramita, the prajna paramita, or perfection of wisdom.
Razala began the series by talking about the paramita of dana, generosity.
How can one be wise without a generous heart?
The second paramita is called sila in Sanskrit; it is about ethical conduct.
I know no one in this room is unfamiliar with the notion of ethics.
We all grew up with some.
Think for a moment about the ethical practices you were introduced to in your childhood.
What are some of them?
I'm inviting you to just call out: don't lie, be reliable, the golden rule, do unto others as you would have them do unto you, don't call people an asshole, do not speak to others.
So we've had this since we were able to understand what our parents were saying to us or whoever it was that was giving us these guidelines.
Norman Fischer wrote a book on the paramitas that I have drawn from and which Razala is going to expand upon in a further class on the paramitas.
His book is called *The World Could Be Otherwise*, and in it he suggests that the ethics described in the second paramita are a somewhat different take.
On page 55 of the book, he says the bodhisattva's perfection of ethical conduct isn't the usual sort of ethical conduct.
It's ethical conduct beyond ethical, wisdom beyond wisdom.
At first, it involves some intentional restraint when we're getting it together.
But as bodhisattvas continue the path, they easily and spontaneously practice it without particularly noticing.
At this point, the perfection of ethical conduct isn't uptight or restrictive; it's a joyful path of doing what comes naturally out of the fullness of the heart.
We don't generally think of ethical conduct that way.
We think of it quite soberly as a matter of restraint, purification, and righteousness.
You follow ethical guidelines to clean up your act, straighten out your behavior, be a decent and good person.
All good.
And we want to make sure that we're doing all of this less to be a good person and that's the end of it, and more about how that's going to mean to everybody else.
Of course, bodhisattvas do all that.
It just becomes a path of joy again from Norman.
And they know above all that there is no them without everyone else.
So conducting themselves with respect for others is common sense.
And when they mess up, as they sometimes do, as I sometimes do, as you sometimes do, pay attention and make corrections.
Yet the perfection of ethical conduct, like an eagle in flight, soars far beyond conventional ethics into the empty blue skies of love and delight.
And I'm so glad he brought those words in, all of which is to say that, like everything else, the practice of ethics is empty.
Empty of a separate sense of self.
So we aren't doing it just for us.
It reminds me of something John Wiley said about his flight of nerves before his shuso finale.
The hosanchiki, which is the ceremony where everybody lines up and asks an unrehearsed question for an unrehearsed answer, was getting to him.
And he confessed to Norman that he was really nervous and was considering ducking out the back door.
Norman said, "Practice, be there, so that others may practice, too."
When I was in my mid-twenties, I was a hippie.
They say once a hippie, always a hippie, so I suppose I still am.
But we wanted to save the world.
Not everyone in that culture, however, was entirely upright.
And I had made friends with a guy who owned a head shop in Minneapolis.
Very exciting, very cool.
Leather products, tie-dye, and a little drugs thrown in.
At one point, he asked me if I wanted to make some money, big money.
I would transport cocaine from South America back home.
He thought I would be good because I was teaching school at the time, and I had that teacher persona in the midst of it all.
I actually considered it for about five minutes: school loans gone, you know, everything.
And then I thought about my grandpa.
He was still alive, and we had a great relationship.

But beyond that idea for myself and my safety, the risk of being caught and jailed, I knew that I couldn't risk hurting him, perhaps never seeing him again, and letting him down from all the good he had given to me.
What the effect would be on others was equally important to the danger to myself.
Norman goes on, "Ongoing meditative practice makes this correction even more obvious.
You see that you never get away with anything, that shoddy conduct casts shadows on your mind and heart, that you feel sooner or later as mental or physical discomfort when you sit down to meditate."
I'm reminded of a story in one of the persona books that I read early on.
One of the students of my first, I guess my first teacher, Goenka, was someone who had developed bombs, atomic energy.
He was in a cell, a single cell of meditation, and the story is that he was just bouncing off the walls, subtle, discharging all of that.
So this framework for ethical conduct in Zen, if you haven't already figured it out, is through studying the 16 Bodhisattva precepts.
It's a lifelong study and practice once you have embraced it.
Some people choose to make a formal course of preparation in order to really commit to the precepts.
We spend about a year in study.
While at Red Cedar, we offer the precepts study to everyone who is interested.

There are always at least a few people who are immersed in the precepts study in preparation for taking the formal Bodhisattva vow, sewing a rakusu, and who are participating more actively in the sangha.
My first precept study was like this.

After asking to study the precepts, I just kind of walked up to the teacher and said, "I want to study the precepts with you," and he went, "Well, it's kind of not exactly how we do it, you know, we kind of want to get the know-it-first, and I need to get up a group that is going to be worth it to do it for."
So three years later, I got a letter in the mail inviting me to study the precepts.
That was after many, many visits and sessions and all that.
Anyway, there were 11 of us, and we did it together in Canada.
We met once a month as a group, and in between we studied as a partner, one precept at a time.
We spent a weekend at one practitioner's home starting to sew our rakasus.
We became a cohesive group.
These are the precepts: the three refuges.
"I take refuge in Buddha.
We just did this.
I take refuge in Dharma.
I take refuge in Sangha."
The three pure precepts: "I vow to refrain from harmful conduct.
I vow to cultivate beneficial conduct.
I vow to benefit all beings."
And then the ten clear mind precepts, and these precepts have been originally known as prohibitive precepts: "Don't do this, don't do that."
But more recently within this, say, a hundred-year period or less, there's been a movement toward clear mind precepts where we try to put a little more positive spin.
So when I say these, I'll first say the clear mind precept and then I'll say the original prohibitive precept.
Prohibitive precept: "I vow to protect life, not to kill.
I vow to receive gifts, not to steal.
I vow to respect others, not to misuse sexuality.
I vow to be truthful, not to lie.
I vow to remain clear, not to intoxicate self or others.
I vow to practice generosity, not to be possessive of anything.
I vow to practice loving kindness, not to harbor ill will.
I vow to cherish and polish the three treasures."
Now, while these precepts are strong statements, they are flexible.
Each precept may be viewed on levels or perspectives: concrete or relative, compassionate and absolute.
For example, the second of the ten clear mind precepts reads, "I vow to receive gifts, not to steal."
From a concrete point of view, we vow to refrain from taking something that isn't ours.
But what about the man whose family is starving, who walks by the back door of a bakery?
Is one loaf of bread for a starving family truly breaking a precept?
From a compassionate point of view, children must eat or they will sicken and die.
On an absolute level, there's no difference between giver, receiver, and gift.
All of this requires both discernment and flexibility and a devotion to upright living.

On page 57 of *This World Could Be Otherwise*, Norman says, "Although we have all become adept at presenting ourselves to the world as if we were upstanding citizens in good shape, in fact, none of us is what we have become adept at seeming to be.
Everyone is more tentative, more vulnerable, and rougher than they appear.
Accepting this, you are kinder to yourself and everyone else."
This kindness, based on a grounded understanding of human nature, is the root of ethical conduct.
Keep that all the time.
In addition to the precepts, there are a few concepts related to ethics that we cannot leave out: karma, renunciation and atonement, forgiveness and love.
With regarding karma, Norman says, "If blank, then blank."
Karma is the result of actions; it is cause and effect.
In Zen, since we do not tend to dwell on reincarnation from life to life, we view it within this life, moment to moment: how will this action affect my, our, our world's future?
In a timeless view, the vow of repentance, "all my ancient twisted karma, reflects the infinite nature of beginningless greed, hate and delusion.
We pick it up from all time."
It doesn't make it right, but it does absolve us from inventing new karma.
Forgiveness.
Formal Zen doesn't use the word love much, but if it is not at the foundation of our understanding of the world, how can we behave ethically?
If we love incompletely when it only goes one way, like the infatuation of a big crush, whether the crush knows it or not, it has to come from within to infinity and back.
So with the concept firmly embedded, even though everything is in motion, we can't live ethically if we hold grudges or carry old stories about others and about ourselves.
To love fully includes forgiveness.
I didn't see the Grammys, but I understand that Bad Bunny, when he got his award, suggested that in light of present conditions in our society, we cannot reflect hatred back and expect to win.
The only way we can win is with love.
So I might have set a record here for a time of Dharma talk, but I thought we could talk together and then talk with each other.
Let's get into groups of three, and I will ask you to talk about a question.
And here's the question: How does ethical conduct appear as a challenge in your life?
A second question: How do ethics help you?
So choose your group of three, and let's take—we have plenty of time, let's take five minutes each.
